questions.prompt: How many server failures can a six-server Raft cluster tolerate while still making progress?
questions.explanation: A majority of 6 is 4, so the cluster keeps working with 2 servers down. Three is tempting because it is half of six, but with 3 down only 3 remain, which is not more than half, so no leader can be elected and nothing can commit.

questions.prompt: A five-server cluster partitions into {S1, S2} and {S3, S4, S5}. S1 was the leader. What happens on S1's side?
options: S1 keeps committing entries because it is still the legitimate leader
S1 and S2 elect a new leader for a higher term
S1 may append entries to its log but cannot commit any of them
S1 immediately deletes its log to avoid conflicts
questions.explanation: Committing needs acknowledgements from a majority (3 of 5), and S1 can reach only S2. It can still append entries locally, but they stay uncommitted and may later be overwritten. It cannot win a new election either, for the same counting reason.

questions.prompt: Which of these faults falls outside Raft's failure model?
options: A server crashes and restarts with its disk intact
A network switch drops and reorders packets for a minute
A data centre link fails, splitting the cluster into two groups
A server's disk is silently reverted to an old backup and it rejoins the cluster
questions.explanation: Raft tolerates crash-recover servers, lossy networks and partitions. A server whose persistent state has been rolled back may vote twice in a term or forget entries it acknowledged, which is effectively Byzantine behaviour and can break safety.
